findings.title: MarketFactory.updateExtension() Missing Access Control Allows Global Operator Injection
findings.description: The updateExtension() function in MarketFactory.sol has no access modifier (missing onlyOwner). Any address can call updateExtension(attacker, true) to register itself as a global extension, which grants isOperator = true for ALL accounts across ALL markets via the authorization() function at line 84. The attacker can then call Market.update() to withdraw all collateral from every user in every market via negative collateral, which sends withdrawn funds to msg.sender. Compare with updateParameter() (line 92) and updateReferralFee() (line 195) which both have onlyOwner. Complete protocol TVL is at risk with two trivial function calls.

findings.title: Market.claimFee() Sends Tokens to msg.sender Instead of Account Owner
findings.description: The claimFee function sends accumulated fees (protocol, oracle, risk, claimable) to msg.sender via token.push(msg.sender, ...) at line 322, not to the account owner. Any authorized operator can claim all fees on behalf of an account and receive them directly. This is a design-level trust issue where operator approval for position management also grants fee-claiming ability.

findings.title: MetaQuants Immutable Single Signer With No Rotation Mechanism
findings.description: The MetaQuantsFactory uses a single immutable ECDSA signer address set at construction time. If the signing key is compromised, there is no rotation mechanism. All MetaQuants oracles become permanently vulnerable to price manipulation. Full factory redeployment and oracle migration across all markets is required for remediation.

findings.title: Coordinator.claimFee() Passes Wrong Account - Risk Fees Permanently Locked
findings.description: Coordinator.claimFee() calls market.claimFee(msg.sender) where msg.sender is the comptroller address, but Market requires account == coordinator (the Coordinator contract address) to release risk fees. This is a clear functional bug: risk fees accumulate in every coordinated market but can never be claimed through the intended path. Requires contract upgrade to fix.

findings.title: Adiabatic Fee Net-Zero Property Breaks Under Socialization
findings.description: Adiabatic fees compute based on book position skew, not socialized effective position. Under socialization, users who opened at one skew level cannot close at the same level, breaking the net-zero fee property. Confirmed via numerical calculation: open 100 at skew 0->100 (fee=+500), socialized to effective 50, close 50 at skew 100->50 (fee=-375). Net surplus of +125 stays in the system, overcharging the socialized user.
findings.location: Adiabatic fee computation in VersionLib and AdiabaticMath6

findings.title: Vault _socialize Accounting Desynchronization During Insolvency
findings.description: When totalCollateral < 0 (vault insolvency), _socialize() returns 0 via UFixed6Lib.unsafeFrom() clamping, but _update() at line 311 still decrements global.assets by the full claimAssets amount. Users' accounting entries are cleared without receiving tokens and global.assets desynchronizes from actual token balance. First claimers during insolvency permanently remove assets from the ledger, reducing what later claimers can receive even if solvency recovers.

findings.title: Coordinator Can Force Liquidations via Instant Risk Parameter Manipulation
findings.description: No timelock exists on updateRiskParameter(). A coordinator can increase maintenance to 99%, liquidate all positions collecting liquidation fees, then restore maintenance. No timelock, no delay, no grace period for users to add collateral or close positions. Combined with scale=0 bricking (VULN-106) and tiny scale confiscatory fees (VULN-107), coordinators have unchecked power over user funds.

findings.title: Oracle Provider Switch Without Price Consistency Validation
findings.description: Oracle factory owner can instantly switch oracle providers without price consistency validation between old and new providers. Only checks global.current == global.latest (no mid-switch). A malicious switch could feed manipulated prices causing mass liquidations. All pending orders settle at the price from the new provider.

findings.title: Pause Blocks All Operations With No Emergency Withdrawal Mechanism
findings.description: When MarketFactory is paused, settle() and update() are both blocked via whenNotPaused modifier with no emergency withdrawal mechanism. User funds are permanently frozen if the pauser is compromised. No time-limited pause exists. claimFee() still works during pause, allowing the protocol to extract fees while users cannot withdraw. Same issue affects Vault via VaultFactory pause.

findings.title: Vault Lacks ReentrancyGuard Entirely
findings.description: Vault.sol does not inherit ReentrancyGuard and has no nonReentrant on any function. During _update(): asset.pull() then _manage() then asset.push() then _saveContext(). State is not saved until after all external calls. Read-only reentrancy risk for integrated protocols reading totalAssets()/convertToShares() during a callback window where state is inconsistent.

findings.title: Intent Price Override Has No Bounds Relative to Oracle Price
findings.description: Guarantee.notional (intent price override) has no validation against the oracle price. The difference between oracle price and intent price creates unbounded PnL for the signer at the expense of the maker pool. Combined with solver self-dealing (VULN-073), this enables systematic extraction from makers. No maxDeviation or slippage check exists.

findings.title: MultiInvoker _commitPrice Silently Swallows Oracle Failures
findings.description: When revertOnFailure is false, oracle commit failures are silently swallowed in _commitPrice(). An attacker can construct a MultiInvoker batch where Action 1 is COMMIT_PRICE with revertOnFailure=false (silently fails), followed by Action 2 UPDATE_POSITION using the stale oracle price. Enables position manipulation at favorable stale prices.

findings.title: KeeperOracle Unbounded Callback Set Inflates Settlement Fees
findings.description: The _localCallbacks EnumerableSet grows unboundedly per version. Settlement fee scales with callback count. Many unique accounts requesting at the same timestamp inflate fees charged to all users during settlement. Can be used as a griefing vector to cause excessive fee extraction from innocent users.

findings.title: Implementation Contracts Can Be Initialized by Anyone
findings.description: Implementation contracts behind beacon proxies (Market, KeeperOracle, Oracle, Vault, Account) can be initialized by anyone directly. Standard practice is to call _disableInitializers() in the constructor. While this doesn't affect proxy instances, initialized implementations could confuse integrators or be used in social engineering attacks.

findings.title: Complete Vault Freeze When Any Single Market Is Paused
findings.description: The Vault iterates through all registered markets during _settleUnderlying(), _loadContext(), and _manage(). If any single registered market is paused (whenNotPaused on settle/update), the entire vault operation reverts. No mechanism exists to skip paused markets or deregister them. A single paused market freezes the entire vault, affecting all depositors across all markets.

findings.title: Silent Order Overwrite Enables Front-Running of Keeper Execution
findings.description: _placeOrder stores new orders at user-specified orderId without checking if the existing order is pending execution. A user watching the mempool can see a keeper's executeOrder transaction and front-run it by overwriting the order with a different one (e.g., changing position delta or collateral). The keeper executes the modified order unknowingly.

findings.title: USDC Blacklisting Permanently Locks All Account Funds
findings.description: If an Account contract address is USDC-blacklisted, all funds are permanently locked. The Account's wrapIfNecessary and unwrap functions require USDC transfers, and DSU redemption also requires USDC. Since Account addresses are deterministic (CREATE2), targeted blacklisting is possible. No fallback mechanism exists to rescue funds via alternative token paths.

findings.title: LinearAdiabatic6 scale=0 Permanently Bricks Market
findings.description: If a coordinator sets takerFee.scale or makerFee.scale to 0, the adiabatic fee calculation divides by scale, causing a division-by-zero revert in settlement. This permanently blocks settlement for all positions in that market. Since settlement is required for any operation, the market is effectively bricked with no recovery mechanism without factory owner intervention.

findings.title: No Sequencer Uptime Check on L2 Deployments
findings.description: No Chainlink sequencer uptime oracle check across all L2 oracle and keeper systems. During sequencer downtime, block.timestamp stops advancing. On restart, timestamps jump forward, potentially causing stale oracle prices to be used for settlements. Affects all L2 deployments on Arbitrum, Optimism, and Base.
findings.location: All L2 oracle and keeper systems

findings.title: Self-Liquidation Avoids Trade Fees and Captures Liquidation Fee
findings.description: Protected (liquidation) orders bypass InvariantLib checks. Self-liquidation via a second account allows a user to: (1) let their position become barely under-collateralized, (2) use a second account to liquidate themselves, (3) avoid trade fees on the position close, (4) capture the liquidation fee via the second account. Net effect is closing a position without trade fees while earning a liquidation fee.

findings.title: Front-Running Oracle Commits for Favorable Settlement
findings.description: Pyth prices are publicly observable off-chain before on-chain commitment. Users can observe oracle prices and place orders that will settle at known prices. The async settlement model mitigates this partially, but the timing window creates information asymmetry, particularly exploitable when combined with oracle version gaps where multiple versions settle at once.
findings.location: Oracle commit timing in Pyth integration

findings.title: Global Fee Bucket uint48 Overflow Causes Market DoS
findings.description: Global.sol stores protocolFee, oracleFee, and riskFee as uint48 values (max ~281M USDC in Fixed6). Fees accumulate monotonically in GlobalLib.update() and the store() function reverts if any value exceeds uint48 max. A busy market where fees are not regularly claimed can hit this ceiling, freezing all market operations.

findings.title: cancelGroupWithSignature Allows Unauthorized Group Cancellation
findings.description: The cancelGroupWithSignature function verifies a signature against common.signer but cancels the group for common.account. No check ensures the signer is authorized to act on behalf of the account. An attacker can sign a GroupCancellation with their own key, setting account=victim, to cancel any victim's group nonces, invalidating batches of pending signed messages.

findings.title: Operator Collateral Withdrawal Sends Funds to Operator Not Account Owner
findings.description: Collateral withdrawals are sent to msg.sender (the operator), not the account owner in Market._update(). Combined with global operator scope, any approved operator can extract all of a user's collateral across all markets. This is by design but creates significant trust assumptions that are not well-documented.

findings.title: Socialization Frontrunning Enables First-Mover Advantage During Insolvency
findings.description: During vault insolvency, early claimers receive a proportionally larger share of remaining collateral. An attacker who detects impending insolvency can front-run settlement to claim first, receiving more than their fair share. Somewhat mitigated by async settlement but still exploitable with market-watching bots.

findings.title: Partial Market Failure in Vault _manage() Causes Full Vault DoS
findings.description: If any single underlying market's _retarget() call reverts (e.g., market paused, position limits hit, high utilization), all vault operations are blocked for all users. This creates a denial-of-service amplified by multi-market dependency where one problematic market locks all vault funds.

findings.title: Share Price Manipulation via Direct Token Donation to Vault
findings.description: An attacker can inflate vault share price by directly depositing collateral into an underlying market on behalf of the vault address, inflating totalCollateral. This affects totalAssets() and consequently share pricing. Partially mitigated by VaultFactory's anti-inflation initial deposit, but effectiveness depends on initialAmount size.

findings.title: Weight Update During Pending Orders Causes Accounting Mismatch
findings.description: Changing market weights while pending deposit/redeem orders exist causes the checkpoint's spread calculation to use fees from positions adjusted to new weights, but orders were priced under old weights. This creates accounting discrepancies and unfair fee distribution between users who deposited before vs. after weight changes.

findings.title: Settlement Fee Not Capped by maxSettlementFee During Commit
findings.description: The OracleParameter.maxSettlementFee field exists but is never enforced at fee computation time. Settlement fees are computed from volatile gas oracle data without any cap. During gas spikes on L2s, fees could far exceed intended maximums, draining user collateral disproportionately.

findings.title: Keeper Commit Fee Replication for Shared Underlying Feeds
findings.description: When multiple oracle IDs share the same underlying feed, the data cost is replicated per oracle ID. The keeper pays once for the underlying data but gets compensated N times (once per oracle ID). Creates systematic keeper over-compensation at the expense of users paying settlement fees.

findings.title: Async Settlement Fee Double-Spending Between Commit and Settle
findings.description: The commit() function claims asyncFee * callbacks at commit time based on current callback count, while settle() pays asyncFee per callback from the shared KeeperOracle balance without per-version tracking. Cross-version balance sharing could cause settle() to revert for some callbacks if balance is insufficient.

findings.title: Manager Order Replacement Race Condition With Keeper Execution
findings.description: Active trigger orders can be silently overwritten without explicit cancellation, creating race conditions with keeper execution. A delegated signer could replace a user's stop-loss with different trigger conditions while the keeper is attempting execution, potentially leaving the user without intended downside protection.

findings.title: MultiInvoker EXEC_ORDER Bypasses Invoke-Level Authorization
findings.description: The EXEC_ORDER action in MultiInvoker is permissionless by design but has an inconsistent authorization model. The outer account parameter serves no purpose for the EXEC_ORDER action, making the authorization model confusing and potentially exploitable if future code changes assume account-level authorization applies.

findings.title: RebalanceLib Returns canRebalance=false for Zero-Collateral Markets
findings.description: When a market's collateral is zero (e.g., after liquidation), RebalanceLib.checkMarket() returns canRebalance=false regardless of the target allocation. This prevents rebalancing funds into the empty market, creating a dead state where the entire rebalance group is broken and cannot recover automatically.

findings.title: Missing Chainlink Oracle Staleness Validation in Kept/GasOracle
findings.description: Both Kept.sol and GasOracle.sol call Chainlink's latestRoundData() discarding roundId, startedAt, updatedAt, and answeredInRound. No staleness check and no answer>0 check. A stale/zero ETH price zeroes keeper fees (griefing keepers) or inflates them (extracting user collateral). Affects MultiInvoker, Controller_Incentivized, Manager, and all L2 variants.

findings.title: Empty Calldata Means L1 Data Fee Not Compensated for Keepers
findings.description: All production call sites pass msg.data[0:0] (empty calldata) to _handleKeeperFee(). On Arbitrum, only the 140-byte fixed overhead is included; actual calldata cost is ignored. Missing Controller_Optimism and Manager_Optimism means no L1 fee compensation on OP Stack at all. Keepers are systematically under-compensated for L1 data posting costs.

findings.title: Oracle Price Commit Sandwiching via MultiInvoker Batch
findings.description: MultiInvoker allows COMMIT_PRICE + UPDATE_POSITION in one transaction. While async settlement prevents direct sandwich attacks on the attacker's own orders, the attacker controls which Pyth price is committed for a given version, affecting other users' pending orders. A malicious keeper can selectively commit prices that maximize their own PnL.

findings.title: Coordinator.claimFee Sweeps Entire Token Balance
findings.description: Coordinator.claimFee() calls market.token().push(comptroller) which pushes the ENTIRE token balance of the Coordinator contract, not just the claimed fee amount. If the Coordinator holds tokens from multiple markets or other sources, a single claimFee call for one market sweeps all residual tokens to the comptroller.

findings.title: Missing Controller_Optimism and Manager_Optimism L2 Variants
findings.description: Controller_Arbitrum and Manager_Arbitrum exist with L2-specific gas handling, but no Controller_Optimism or Manager_Optimism exist. On OP Stack chains, the base Kept contract's _calldataFee() returns ZERO, meaning keepers on Optimism/Base receive no L1 data fee compensation for Controller and Manager operations, making those operations unprofitable.

findings.title: KeeperOracle Timeout Causes Stale Price Carry-Over on L2
findings.description: KeeperOracle carries over latestPrice when timeout is exceeded. On L2, block.timestamp jumps discontinuously after sequencer restart. The timeout check triggers prematurely, causing a potentially very stale price to be used for settlement (marked as valid=false). No L2 timestamp awareness exists in the timeout logic.

findings.title: Oracle Version Gaps Cause Large Single-Block PnL Events
findings.description: When oracle versions are skipped (keeper doesn't commit for several versions), the next committed version settles ALL pending orders at once. If the price moved significantly during the gap, this creates large single-block PnL events. Keepers have no obligation to commit every version and can selectively commit only profitable ones.

findings.title: Liquidation Fee Can Exceed Account Collateral Creating Bad Debt
findings.description: Liquidation fee equals position * liquidationFee rate. If the position is large relative to remaining collateral (high leverage near liquidation threshold), the liquidation fee can exceed remaining collateral. The excess becomes bad debt socialized across the market, exacerbated by oracle version gaps where price moves make accounts deeply underwater.

findings.title: Vault Uses Minimum Timestamp Creating Stale Valuation
findings.description: Vault uses the minimum timestamp across all underlying markets for checkpoint completion. If one market settles before another, the vault uses the earliest timestamp, creating stale valuation for markets that have already settled at a more recent price. This affects share/asset ratio calculation and deposit/redemption pricing.

findings.title: Version Storage int48 Packing Overflow Risk
findings.description: Version struct packs accumulator values into int48 (range ~+/-140M at 6 decimals). These are cumulative values that grow over time. High-volume or long-running markets can exceed int48 bounds, causing VersionStorageInvalidError and permanently blocking settlement. The int64 value accumulators (~+/-$9.22M per unit) are also a concern for high-value markets.

findings.title: Funding Rate PID Controller Manipulation via Skew
findings.description: PController6 funding rate is proportional to skew. An attacker with sufficient capital can open a large long to skew the funding rate, then open an offsetting short via a separate account. The net cost is trade fees, while other shorts in the market also receive elevated funding. Cost-effective when position is large relative to existing market positions.

findings.title: Settlement Fee Dilution via Many Small Orders
findings.description: Settlement fees are split equally among all orders in a version. An attacker can place many small orders in the same version, diluting the per-order settlement fee (each pays settlementFee/N instead of the full fee). This under-compensates keepers and is bounded only by maxPendingLocal/maxPendingGlobal limits.

findings.title: Intent Order Price Override Enables Solver Profit Extraction
findings.description: Intent orders set a price override (Guarantee.notional). The difference between actual oracle price and intent price flows as PnL. A solver who is also the intent signer can time intents to maximize price override PnL, effectively front-running oracle updates. The intent.fee caps at 100% but the price override PnL is unbounded.

findings.title: Vault Deposit/Redemption Oracle Timing Attack
findings.description: Vault checkpoint completion uses market collateral at the checkpoint timestamp. Since Pyth prices are publicly observable before on-chain commitment, an attacker can observe the next price and deposit before favorable commit or redeem before unfavorable commit. VaultExistingOrderError limits to one action per oracle version but value can still be extracted from passive depositors.
findings.location: Vault deposit/redemption pricing via checkpoint completion

findings.title: First Depositor Vault Share Inflation Attack
findings.description: Classic first-depositor attack on vault share pricing. First depositor mints 1 share then donates a large amount to inflate share price, causing subsequent depositors to receive 0 shares due to rounding. The vault has an anti-inflation initial deposit mechanism, but if the initialAmount is small, the attack may still be economical.

findings.title: Vault Rebalancing Front-Running via Weight Change Observation
findings.description: Vault rebalancing is permissionless. Weight changes trigger rebalancing of collateral across markets. An attacker can observe weight update transactions in the mempool, open positions in markets about to receive more collateral, and profit from the additional liquidity. Bounded by async settlement but still creates a MEV opportunity.

findings.title: Accumulator Division-by-Zero Relies on Implicit Fee-Count Coupling
findings.description: Accumulator6 divides by position count. When count is zero, div-by-zero reverts. The codebase relies on implicit coupling: fee = count * rate, so when count=0, fee=0, and the isZero() early return prevents the division. A future code change computing non-zero fee with zero count would halt settlement. Fragile pattern that should be made explicit.

findings.title: Rounding Direction Exploits in Accumulator6
findings.description: Accumulator6 uses truncation (toward zero) for all division operations, systematically under-charging fees. Traders making many small trades can exploit the per-trade rounding to their advantage, with cumulative savings growing with trade count. Consistently favors the fee payer over the fee receiver.

findings.title: Guarantee System Settlement Fee Avoidance
findings.description: Guarantee orders (from intents) create paired orders that may distribute settlement fees differently than regular orders. When a guarantee order is matched with a regular order in the same version, the settlement fee distribution may be skewed, allowing participants to avoid their fair share of settlement costs.

findings.title: Vault Checkpoint Socialization Claim Race
findings.description: Vault checkpoint completion determines share/asset ratio. If the vault experiences a loss during settlement, users who claim immediately after checkpoint completion get the post-loss ratio, while users who deposited in earlier versions may have claims valued using outdated ratios. The vault lacks a re-pricing mechanism for in-flight claims.

findings.title: Immutable External References With No Upgrade Path
findings.description: ChainlinkFactory's chainlink, feeManager, and feeTokenAddress are all immutable; PythFactory's pyth is immutable. If these external protocols upgrade their infrastructure or change contract addresses, the factories become unusable and require full redeployment plus oracle migration. No upgrade path exists for changing external dependencies.

findings.title: Fixed6/Fixed18 mul/div/muldiv Intermediate Overflow
findings.description: Fixed6.mul computes a*b/BASE where a*b can overflow int256. Fixed6.div computes a*BASE/b with the same issue. No OpenZeppelin Math.mulDiv is used. Causes revert (not silent corruption) due to Solidity 0.8.x checked arithmetic, but can DoS settlement paths for markets with large accumulated values.

findings.title: Keeper Can Selectively Delay Oracle Commits to Force Invalidation
findings.description: Keepers have discretion over when to commit oracle versions. A malicious keeper can selectively delay commits past the timeout window, forcing KeeperOracle to fall back to latestPrice and mark the version as invalid. This affects all traders whose orders were pending for that version. The keeper still receives compensation for the delayed commit.
findings.location: KeeperOracle commit timing and timeout logic

findings.title: Settlement Fee Charged on Invalidated Oracle Versions
findings.description: When an oracle version is invalidated (timeout exceeded), orders pending for that version are still charged settlement fees but their positions are not opened/closed. Traders pay for settlement that didn't settle their position and must re-submit and pay again. Combined with selective keeper delay (VULN-065), enables fee griefing.
findings.location: Settlement fee handling for invalid versions

findings.title: Market.claimExposure() CEI Violation
findings.description: claimExposure() performs token push/pull BEFORE zeroing exposure in storage, and lacks nonReentrant modifier (present on settle/update but missing here). Violates checks-effects-interactions pattern. If the token ever supports callbacks (ERC777), the owner could re-enter and double-claim exposure. Currently mitigated by onlyOwner + DSU being standard ERC20.

findings.title: Solver Can Fill Intent Against Itself (Self-Dealing)
findings.description: No validation prevents a solver from using their own account as counterparty when filling intents. A solver controlling both signer and counterparty accounts can create intents with extreme price overrides, fill them against themselves, and extract value from the maker pool. Combined with unbounded price override (VULN-072), this is a systematic extraction vector.

findings.title: Risk Parameter Changes Apply Retroactively to Pending Orders
findings.description: updateRiskParameter() writes to storage immediately and settlement reads current risk params, not params at order placement time. A user opens a position with 5% maintenance, coordinator changes to 50%, and the user is immediately under-collateralized on settlement. No snapshot of risk params at order creation time exists. Exacerbated by lack of timelock.

findings.title: Vault _settle Skips Intermediate Local Checkpoints
findings.description: Vault._settle uses a while loop for global settlement but only a single if statement for local settlement. If a user has multiple pending checkpoints (current > latest + 1), only the most recent is settled. Intermediate checkpoints are skipped, leading to incorrect share/asset calculations that miss intermediate fee adjustments.

findings.title: RiskParameter Storage Truncation Bypasses Validation
findings.description: RiskParameter storage uses .truncate() for makerLimit, makerFee.scale, and takerFee.scale, dropping fractional 6-decimal parts. The validate function checks pre-truncation values but post-truncation values are stored. A coordinator could pass validation with one value but store a different (truncated) value that might violate the intended check.

findings.title: MultiInvoker Referrer Selection Ignores interfaceFee2 Receiver
findings.description: MultiInvoker's _update passes referrer to market.update() using priority logic where interfaceFee1.receiver takes precedence. If both fees have non-zero receivers, only interfaceFee1.receiver is used as the referrer. interfaceFee2.receiver receives their interface fee but is NOT credited as a market referrer, losing expected referral revenue.

findings.title: KeeperOracle settle() asyncFee Not Properly Accounted
findings.description: KeeperOracle.settle() pushes asyncFee per callback from the market's token balance (not from an earmarked pool). The full settlement fee is claimed during commit() but settle() independently pushes asyncFee from market.token(). If the market token balance is reduced between commit and settle calls, the settle could push improperly accounted tokens or fail.

findings.title: VerifierBase Rejects Valid EIP-1271 Smart Contract Signatures
findings.description: VerifierBase enforces signature.length == 65, preventing smart contract wallets (Gnosis Safe, Argent, etc.) from using non-standard signature lengths. While the contract uses SignatureChecker.isValidSignatureNow which supports EIP-1271, the length check blocks this path entirely. Users with smart contract wallets cannot use signed intent orders or verified messages.

findings.title: Accumulator Rounding Causes Systematic Value Leakage
findings.description: The Accumulator6 pattern divides accumulated values by position count, truncating remainders. These remainders represent value permanently locked in the market contract and never distributed to any participant. While individually immaterial per epoch, this compounds over the lifetime of the market, creating a persistent drain on the value conservation invariant.

findings.title: No Hard Invariant Check for maker >= max(long, short)
findings.description: The protocol does not enforce maker >= max(long, short) as a hard invariant. Instead, socialization is used as a fallback. When maker < major side, PnL is socialized (capped). This creates non-obvious PnL dynamics where users may receive less than expected, and positions can enter a socialized state without explicit warning to users.
findings.location: Market and InvariantLib position invariant checks

findings.title: Orders Get Stuck if Oracle Provider Fails to Commit a Version
findings.description: The Market settlement loop requires oracle's latestVersion.timestamp >= order.timestamp. If an oracle provider fails to commit a requested version, orders at that timestamp block settlement until the oracle commits or advances past it. Pending orders accumulate, potentially hitting maxPendingGlobal/maxPendingLocal limits and blocking new orders entirely.

findings.title: Pre-Fee Margin Check Gap Allows Under-Collateralization
findings.description: InvariantLib.validate checks margin against collateral AFTER deposit but BEFORE fees are deducted (fees are deducted during settlement). A user can pass the margin check, but after trade fees, linear fees, proportional fees, and adiabatic fees are deducted at settlement, collateral may fall below maintenance. Creates a window for immediately-liquidatable positions.

findings.title: Front-Runnable Re-initialization Functions on MultiInvoker and OracleFactory
findings.description: MultiInvoker has initializer(2) and OracleFactory has initializer(3). These re-initialization functions are not behind factory patterns and can be front-run during upgrades. Anyone who calls MultiInvoker.initialize() before the deployer could set ethOracle_ to a malicious address, inflating keeper compensation via manipulated gas prices.

findings.title: Market.migrate() Has No Explicit Version Guard
findings.description: Market.migrate() relies solely on storage-level double-migration checks without an explicit version guard. If the storage state doesn't prevent re-execution, migration could be called multiple times or in the wrong order. Should include explicit migration versioning to prevent re-application of migration logic.

findings.title: Oracle.register() Allows Re-registration Without Pending Operation Safeguards
findings.description: Oracle.register() allows re-registration of oracle providers without checking for pending operations. If orders are waiting on an oracle version from the current provider, switching providers could strand those orders or cause them to be settled with prices from a different source without users' awareness.

findings.title: Market Deadlock Under Small maxPendingGlobal With Slow Oracle
findings.description: When maxPendingGlobal is small and oracle commits are delayed, pending orders accumulate and hit the limit, blocking new orders from any user. Since settlement requires oracle commit and oracle commit may depend on keeper incentives, a negative feedback loop can form where insufficient activity starves keepers, further delaying commits.
findings.location: Market pending order limits and settlement

findings.title: Vault Bottlenecked by Slowest Market Oracle Settlement Speed
findings.description: The Vault's global settlement loop requires all registered markets to be settled. If one market's oracle is slow or stale, it blocks the vault's global checkpoint advancement, delaying all deposits and redemptions across all markets. Settlement throughput is limited by the slowest oracle provider.

findings.title: No Slippage Protection on Trigger Order Execution After Boundary
findings.description: Manager trigger orders check fillable() with comparison -1 (lte) or 1 (gte) against a price threshold. There is no slippage protection after trigger -- once triggered, the order executes at whatever the next settlement price is, which could be significantly past the trigger price due to gap moves or oracle latency.

findings.title: Double Fee Extraction on Simultaneous Trigger Order Execution
findings.description: If multiple trigger orders for the same account become fillable simultaneously, each execution creates a separate market update with its own settlement fee. A keeper can execute them individually rather than batching, maximizing settlement fee extraction from the user's collateral.

findings.title: Negative Market Collateral Causes Rebalance Revert
findings.description: Controller rebalancing calculates target collateral per market. If a market has negative collateral (underwater position), the rebalance math tries to transfer tokens from the account to bring it to the target, but the account may not have sufficient tokens, causing the entire rebalance to revert and wasting the keeper's gas.

findings.title: Account Contract Missing Operator Authorization for Market Withdrawals
findings.description: Account contract allows market withdrawals without separate operator authorization. Once deployed, the Controller manages rebalancing and operations. If the Controller's operator model doesn't properly scope market-level permissions, authorized operators may be able to withdraw from markets they shouldn't access.

findings.title: Multiple Pending Market Entries From Single Trigger Order Execution
findings.description: When a Manager trigger order is executed, it calls market.update() which creates a pending order. If the user already has pending orders, this adds to the count. Multiple trigger executions in the same epoch could push the user past maxPendingLocal, blocking further operations until settlement catches up.
findings.location: Manager trigger order execution and Market pending limits

findings.title: Reserve Rapid Allocation Changes Cause Expensive Strategy Churn
findings.description: ReserveBase allows rapid allocation changes between strategies (CompoundV3, AaveV3, Noop). Each change triggers expensive deposit/withdrawal operations on the underlying DeFi protocols. Frequent allocation changes by governance cause unnecessary gas waste and potential slippage on large moves. No cooldown exists between changes.

findings.title: Tiny Scale Values Create Confiscatory Proportional and Adiabatic Fees
findings.description: LinearAdiabatic6 and proportional fee calculations use scale as a divisor. Very small scale values (e.g., 1) cause the scaled skew to be enormous, resulting in confiscatory fee levels. A coordinator could set scale to a minimal value, causing all taker orders to pay unreasonably high adiabatic fees. Combined with no timelock (VULN-067), enables instant extraction.
findings.location: Adiabatic/proportional fee computation with small scale

findings.title: claimExposure Missing Reentrancy Guard
findings.description: External call occurs before state update in claimExposure(), but is guarded by onlyOwner and uses standard ERC20 (no callbacks). Defense-in-depth recommendation to add nonReentrant modifier. Currently safe due to DSU being a standard ERC20 without callback hooks.

findings.title: Cross-Market Operator/Signer Scope Too Broad
findings.description: Operators are global, not per-market. Approving an operator grants them access across all markets, amplifying the blast radius of any operator compromise. A design issue that significantly increases trust requirements and should be prominently documented to users.

findings.title: DedupLib O(n^2) Gas Griefing
findings.description: The DedupLib uses an O(n^2) algorithm for deduplication. This is a real gas efficiency concern but is bounded by the registered oracle count. Could be used as a minor griefing vector to increase gas costs for operations that use deduplication.

findings.title: Interface Fee Receivers Unvalidated
findings.description: Operators/signers can set arbitrary interface fee receivers without validation. This is within trust model bounds but lacks any validation that the receiver address is a legitimate fee recipient. Low severity as it's within the operator trust assumption.

findings.title: Keeper Fee Charged Before Signature Verification
findings.description: Keeper fee is computed/charged before signature verification in certain paths. Currently safe due to atomic revert (if verification fails, the entire transaction reverts including the fee). Latent risk if future code changes separate these operations. Defense-in-depth recommendation to verify before charging.

findings.title: Reserve Mint/Redeem Rounding Asymmetry
findings.description: Reserve uses Fixed-point math for mint/redeem conversions. Rounding direction may favor or disfavor users depending on price direction. Low impact due to small dust amounts per transaction, but could compound over many transactions.

findings.title: Fixed6 Intermediate Overflow in Chained Multiplications
findings.description: Fixed6 mul uses int256 intermediates which can overflow for extreme values. Bounded by realistic market parameters and causes revert (not silent corruption) due to Solidity 0.8.x checked arithmetic. Low practical risk in normal market conditions.

findings.title: Keeper Fee Inflation via Gas Measurement and Buffer
findings.description: Keeper fee has immutable multipliers/buffers set at deploy. All production call sites pass empty calldata. Fees are capped by user-signed maxFee. Calldata inflation is not possible in production. Gas measurement is bounded by EVM gasleft(). Low practical risk due to existing caps.

findings.title: PAccumulator Skew Truncation and Precision Loss
findings.description: PAccumulator6 chains three Fixed6 multiplications, each truncating toward zero. For small rates, small time deltas, or small notional values, the chained truncation compounds to significant under-accumulation of funding. Systematic rounding favors the funding-paying side.

findings.title: overrideIfZero Allows Stale Price Injection When Oracle Returns Zero
findings.description: Global.overrideIfZero() substitutes global.latestPrice when the oracle returns a zero price (during transitions or unrequested versions). The latestPrice (stored as int64) could be very stale after long gaps. PnL calculated with the overridden price may be incorrect; price is marked as valid=false but still used for settlement fallback.

findings.title: Vault register() Allows Unbounded Market Registration DoS
findings.description: No upper bound on totalMarkets in Vault.register(). Every vault operation iterates all registered markets. As markets grow, gas costs eventually exceed the block gas limit, making the vault inoperable. While onlyOwner restricts registration, a compromised owner could register many markets to DoS the vault.

findings.title: Controller Keeper Fee Can Fail After Rebalance Drains Account
findings.description: rebalanceGroup modifies collateral positions across markets first, then calls _handleKeeperFee. If rebalancing left the account with insufficient DSU (all deposited to markets), _raiseKeeperFee fails. If the account has neither DSU nor USDC, the entire rebalance transaction reverts, wasting the keeper's gas.

findings.title: Manager TriggerOrder Placement Lacks Market and isSpent Validation
findings.description: _placeOrder stores orders without validating that the market is a valid MarketFactory instance or that isSpent is false. If a user places an order with isSpent=true, it is stored as spent and immediately un-executable/un-cancellable. No validation that the referenced market address is legitimate.

findings.title: Negative Collateral (Bad Debt) Not Checked Until Next Interaction
findings.description: During settlement, collateral can go negative from PnL, but this is only caught at the next _update call via InvariantLib.validate. Between settlements with no interaction, collateral remains negative. Negative collateral represents bad debt that is not socialized and creates an implicit liability in the system.

findings.title: No Storage Gaps in Upgradeable Instance Contracts
findings.description: Critical upgradeable instance contracts (Market, Vault, Oracle, Account) do not include __gap storage arrays. If new storage variables are added in future upgrades, they could collide with storage variables in derived contracts or proxies. Standard practice for UUPS/beacon proxy patterns is to reserve storage slots.
